power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: This study focused on the general adolescent population. All Dutch-speaking adolescents who attended classes in secondary school could participate, regardless of their study track or age. Note that we did not verify in advance whether or not youngsters used IM or not. Indeed, previous research showed that adolescents who do not integrate IM in their daily life, are (almost) non-existent (De Raeymaecker et al., 2025). A sample size estimation was made with the analytic R package "EMAtools" (Kleinman, 2021), that takes the repetitive nature of EMA assessments into account. Given the novel scope of this study, we could not reliably estimate the parameters of the hypothesized population model. In addition, the executed weekend pilot study with 11 participants could not be used either for the purpose of a simulation-based power analysis. According to the power analysis, a minimum of 110 participants (at a 50% "beep" response rate) was necessary to achieve a power of .80, given α = .05 and a small effect size.

text.text: Despite the heightened need of connectedness in adolescence, the association between instant messaging (IM) and its psychosocial outcomes remains ambiguous.

In line with three existing theories on this topic, ecological momentary assessment (one week, 8 prompts/day) was used to link within-person IM behavior and between-person dispositions with the social outcome perceived IM social support and the psychological outcomes loneliness, depressive feelings, and non-suicidal selfinjury (NSSI) behavior.
Furthermore, the interplay between the two was taken into account.
Belgian adolescents (n = 181; Mage = 15.04; 63% women) who reported higher-than-usual IM connection behavior consistently showed better momentary psychosocial outcomes.
Robust differences related to the dispositions could only be identified for depressive feelings.

Women and participants with higher scores on neuroticism, fear of negative evaluation, social anxiety and distress in new situations, and social comparison orientation proved more vulnerable for these feelings.
A tentative association related to loneliness was found for higher neuroticism.
Moreover, age (marginally) strengthened the negative association between IM behavior and the outcomes IM social support and depressive feelings.

In general, these findings highlight the importance of the perceived message content, the potential vulnerability of more extreme dispositions, and the value of embedding psychosocial correlates in a developmental framework.
To this day, the question "Do adolescents benefit from social media?"
cannot be answered unambiguously.
Social media are, because of their persistently changing nature, inherently a moving target (Valkenburg et al., 2016).

text.text: Taking the abovementioned research gaps into account, this EMA study approaches the social and psychological (dis)advantages related to IM conversations between peers from a content-based within-person and a trait-based between-person view.
With this study, we aim to test the accuracy of the interpersonal-connection-behaviors framework, the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypothesis in an adolescent sample.

Accordingly, we will focus on perceived momentary IM social support (i.e., connection behavior) and momentary IM negative social exchange (i.e., disconnection behavior) as proxy for the time-varying content of IM conversations between adolescent peers.
Furthermore, the dispositional traits extraversion, neuroticism, social anxiety and social comparison orientation (SCO) will be taken into account.
Two research question series will be answered, addressing the social respectively the psychological outcomes of IM.
Regarding the social outcomes of IM, we focus on associations related to the same chat conversation.
First, we intent to discover if momentary IM negative social exchange predicts momentary IM social support (i.e., RQ 1A).
We will additionally clarify if the dispositional traits predict between-person differences in the mean level of momentary IM social support (i.e., RQ 1B).
Third, we focus exploratively on the interplay of the mechanisms of the discussed theories.

That is, we aim to unravel whether the dispositional traits predict the strength of the within-person association between momentary IM negative social exchange and momentary IM social support (i.e., RQ 1C).

Concerning the psychological outcomes of IM, three complementary questions will be answered with regard to the mental health outcomes (a) loneliness, (b) depressive feelings, and (c) the presence or absence of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) behavior.
First, we address whether IM social support predicts mental health (i.e., RQ 2A).
In addition, we intend to clarify if the dispositional traits predict between-person differences in the mean level of momentary mental health (i.e., RQ 2B).
Lastly, we focus on the explorative question whether the dispositional traits predict the strength of the within-person association between IM social support and mental health (i.e., RQ 2C).

Bearing in mind the time frame of the corresponding items, we study contemporaneous within-person associations in case of the former two outcomes and concentrate on the temporaneous association in the latter case.
As we aim to evaluate the three aforementioned conflicting frameworks, several conflicting hypotheses are formulated.
These will enable us to establish which of the three is reflected in our data.
Building on the interpersonal-connection-behaviors framework, we anticipate that momentary IM negative social exchange will detract from momentary IM social support.
Moreover, we expect that momentary IM social support will enhance momentary or future mental health.

Regarding the dispositions of the adolescents, the mean level of momentary IM social support and mental health might be predicted by higher (i.e., rich-get-richer effect) or lower levels (i.e., poor-get-richer effect) of extraversion and lower (i.e., rich-get-richer effect) or higher levels (i.e., poor-get-richer effect) of neuroticism, social anxiety, and SCO.
With regard to the exploratory research questions, no explicit hypotheses are put forward.

Given the similarity to the story of Goldilocks, in which the interplay between her personal preferences (i.e., her dispositions) and the available options (i.e., the IM behavior she is confronted with) matter, evidence for the latter will be referred to as a goldilocks effect.
The data of this study were acquired in three data collection periods (July 2024, August 2024, October 2024) with a similar structure.

After a period of recruitment via a follow-up research mailing list (based on previous studies of the lab), distributing flyers to youth movements and mouth-to-mouth advertising, interested adolescents and their parents were invited, during the week before the EMA assessment, to one of the information sessions.

During these online preparatory sessions, all facets of the study were thoroughly explained (e.g., answer surveys as quickly as possible; in case you need to turn off the sound of your phone, make sure you can see its screen).
All items were clarified in order to make sure participants grasped their meaning correctly.
Adolescents who were absent during the online information sessions received the presentation with audio clips.
Afterwards, participants signed an informed assent whereas parents gave permission through an informed consent.
Furthermore, youngsters filled in a cross-sectional baseline questionnaire before entering the EMA phase of the study.

The amount of social support adolescents perceived during their last IM conversation with peer(s) was studied with four items.

text.text: For all research questions covering the social outcomes of IM, we tested two series of contemporaneous RDSEM models based on Bayesian linear regression.
In order to answer RQ1A, we focused on a RDSEM model that included the time-varying constructs IM social support and IM negative social exchange.

text.text: Subsequently, six RDSEM models addressing the effect of the dispositional traits were run with regard to RQ 1B and 1C.

In these models, the dispositional traits extraversion, neuroticism, SCO, and the social anxiety components "Fear of Negative Evaluation" (FNE), "Social Avoidance and Distress-General" (SAD-G), and "Social Avoidance and Distress in New Situations" (SAD-N) were individually introduced in the above-described model.
In all of these models, age and sex 2 were included as covariates.
All dispositions, except sex, were standardized and thus centered.
Furthermore, the latent residual variances were allowed to covariate.
In line with our post-registration, covariation between the random slopes was precluded to reduce the complexity of the model.

To answer our research questions, we were interested in (a) the effects of the dispositional traits on the person-specific mean of IM social support and (b) the effects of dispositional traits on the association between IM negative social exchange and IM social support.

Based on the presumed working mechanisms of two large groups of theories, this study aimed to delineate the social and psychological impact of instant messaging.

While the interpersonalconnection-behaviors framework (Clark et al., 2018) prioritizes the power of (dis)connection behavior, the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypothesis (Kraut et al., 2002) highlights the importance of dispositional traits that remain present across situations.

text.text: In addition, the interplay between the two, in which we analyzed whether the dispositions altered the strength of the association between the IM behavior and the outcome, was taken into account.
In the following text, each of the three mechanisms is discussed.
We robustly found evidence for the predictive power of IM behavior in the prediction of both social and psychological outcomes of instant messaging.
Adolescents who perceived higher levels of IM connection/disconnection behavior compared to their own average, reported better respectively worse social and psychological health.
Only NSSI behavior could not robustly be predicted by the within-person level of IM social support after taking the temporal dynamics of the model into account.
